├── baseline.md            pre-change behavior, captured before implementation
├── results.md             regression findings

findings.title: Baseline NOT CAPTURED areas are required to be restated at verify time, but no verify step, prompt, or template slot implements it
findings.detail: Loop T1's cap behavior mandates 'the verify run must say so rather than implying silence means safety' (loops.md:23), and baseline.template.md:28 repeats 'The verify run must say so explicitly.' Yet nothing in verify mode discharges the obligation: Step 1's instructions (SKILL.md:58-74), the QA Automation Engineer's verify prompt (roles.md:25-38), and results.template.md all lack any mention of NOT CAPTURED — the template's Regression table lists only replayed behaviors and the only honesty section, '## Reduced mode', covers a wholly missing baseline, not a partial one. So a payment flow recorded NOT CAPTURED at baseline reads as clean in results.md and in the verdict's 'Regressions: N' evidence line — silence-implies-safety, the precise failure the skill names. Fix: add a '## Not regression-checked' section to results.template.md sourced from baseline.md's NOT CAPTURED list, and an explicit instruction in Step 1 and the role prompt to carry it forward into the verdict's caveats.
findings.evidence: Those areas cannot be regression-checked later, and the verify run must say so rather than implying silence means safety.

findings.title: Standalone invocation — the likeliest vibe-coder entry — is undefined when plan artifacts do not exist
findings.detail: The skill's own description invites direct use ('Check that the change works and nothing else broke') and it ships as an independently invocable skill on both CLIs, but every verify step hard-depends on upstream artifacts: Step 1's INTENDED requires a `03-design.md` citation, Step 2 iterates `01-intent.md` done-criteria, Step 5 cross-checks `plan.md` `removes:` fields, and the Modes table lists them all as reads (SKILL.md:19). Loop T6 handles exactly one missing artifact — `test/baseline.md` — and nothing else. A user who says 'test my change' without having run explore/plan/implement gets: no criteria to check (Step 2 undefined on an empty set), every difference forced to UNKNOWN (which finding 1 shows goes nowhere), no preflight to diff the suite against (Step 1's second half undefined), and no defined reduced-mode statement for any of it. A world-class process degrades gracefully at its entry points; this one only degrades gracefully at one. Fix: extend T6 (or add a T6b) covering absent plan/intent/design/preflight — state what was missing, derive ad-hoc criteria from the user's stated request, and mark the rest UNVERIFIED.
findings.evidence: description: Check that the change works and nothing else broke — so you know if it is safe to ship.

findings.title: 'Start the real production command and hit a health endpoint' has no isolation, timeout, or teardown guidance
findings.detail: SKILL.md:116 and roles.md:109 instruct the Release Engineer to start the real production process, in a phase that runs largely unattended for a non-expert user. Three unaddressed hazards: (1) production commands read whatever env is present — a vibe coder's `.env`/`.env.production` frequently holds live credentials, and many stacks run migrations or seed jobs on boot, so 'start the real production command' can mutate production data from the test phase of a local pipeline; (2) no timeout or kill instruction — a server that binds a port and never exits hangs the shell in hosts without background-process management; (3) no port-conflict handling against the user's own running dev server, whose failure would be misreported as a broken build. The step's stated goal (build soundness + health) needs an explicit 'run against local/dummy env vars, never production credentials; bounded wait; always kill the process' contract. Compare the care the same step takes with env-var values ('names only, never values') — process-lifecycle and data-safety care is absent.
findings.evidence: Start the real production command and hit a health endpoint.

findings.title: AppSec prompt directs the role to a survey artifact its declared Inputs do not include
findings.detail: The Application Security Engineer is told to compare new endpoints 'against how existing endpoints in this repo do it — the survey recorded the pattern' (roles.md:78), i.e. to consult `02-survey.md`. But its Inputs line (roles.md:70) lists only 'the full change diff, implement/handoff.md, dependency additions'. Under the dispatch contract — subagents receive 'the role prompt plus the named inputs' (host-adapters.md:26) — an isolated-context AppSec subagent structurally cannot perform the comparison as instructed; it will either skip the check or hallucinate the repo's auth pattern. Fix: add `02-survey.md` to the AppSec Inputs line (and to the verify-mode Reads column of SKILL.md's Modes table).
findings.evidence: Compare against how existing endpoints in this repo do it — the survey recorded the pattern.

findings.title: No proportionality: the full 8-15 invocation, expensive-tier pipeline runs identically for a one-line change
findings.detail: Loop budget concedes the cost ('Verify mode runs roughly 8-15 invocations, and the roster itself is not cheap', loops.md:146) but the skill defines no risk-tiered reduced path: a one-line copy fix gets baseline capture, seven verify steps, five roles, deployment-target detection, env-parity tables, and migration analysis. For the declared vibe-coder audience this is the strongest incentive to skip the phase entirely — the worst possible outcome for a safety net. A world-class team scales verification to blast radius (e.g., docs-only or UI-copy changes get criteria + visual + security-lite; schema or auth changes get the full battery). The plan phase already produces the risk signal (files touched, `baseline:`/`removes:` fields, migrations) that a tiering rule could key off. Fix: add an explicit change-class table mapping plan signals to the subset of Steps 1-7 that must run, with everything skipped recorded as SKIPPED — <class rule>, keeping the honesty contract intact.
findings.evidence: Verify mode runs roughly 8–15 invocations, and the roster itself is not cheap.

gaps: No flaky-test or quarantine policy anywhere: nothing distinguishes 'red because broken' from 'red because flaky' — no rerun rule, no stability check at baseline commit time, no quarantine list carried between sessions.

No test-adequacy measure for NEW code: the phase checks stated done-criteria and old behavior (baseline replay), but new logic paths that have neither a criterion nor a pre-existing behavior are never required to be exercised — no changed-line coverage, branch coverage, or mutation check on the diff.

No rollback rehearsal: grokbit-plan mandates a rollback per task and release-readiness.template.md asks 'Reversible: yes', but nothing ever executes a rollback or a down-migration to prove reversibility — a world-class release-readiness check exercises the escape hatch, not just asserts it.

No performance regression check beyond bundle/image size delta: no latency, memory, query-count, or startup-time comparison against baseline, even though the baseline phase is the natural place to capture those numbers.

No accessibility pass in visual QA: the Frontend QA checklist (render, clip, overlap, states) omits contrast, focus order, keyboard reachability, and ARIA — standard items on a world-class FE QA checklist and cheap to add headlessly (e.g., axe-core).

No global cap or escalation rule on test↔implement hand-back round trips: each round has a one-line human approval, but a vibe coder will rubber-stamp; a world-class process escalates to replan (grokbit-plan) after N failed verify rounds the way implement's own 3-deviation rule escalates.

No test-data/fixture strategy for baseline capture: 'exercise the real code path' is silent on auth, seeded databases, and external services beyond the NOT CAPTURED escape hatch — a world-class characterization effort defines how to stand up representative state.

No artifact-hygiene rule for the skill's own outputs: screenshots and verbatim 'observed output' captures can embed PII, tokens, or secrets rendered on screen into .grokbit/plans/<slug>/test/, which the Security step never scans because it scans the change diff, not the test artifacts.
No cross-browser/device dimension in visual verification: one headless engine at two widths is assumed sufficient; no statement of the limit, so a vibe coder reads PASS as 'works everywhere'.

No machine-readable verdict: the extension is named as the one consumer the team controls (host-adapters.md § The Grokbit extension), yet the verdict/severity/counts exist only as prose markdown — a world-class pipeline emits a small structured summary (JSON front-matter or a fixed table) so the UI cannot misparse SHIP WITH CAVEATS.
strengths: Baseline-before-implementation as a hard structural requirement, with retroactive baselining explicitly named and rejected ('A baseline captured after the first edit is not a baseline', SKILL.md:52; 'an instrument calibrated against the thing it is supposed to measure', loops.md:25) — this is correct regression methodology most agent workflows get wrong.

Verification/repair separation enforced at the tool-grant level, not just as advice: roles get no write access to source (roles.md:3), T3 forbids fixing during triage with the rationale that a fix here bypasses Implement's scope audit (loops.md:63), and host-adapters.md:30 shows how to make it a real PreToolUse invariant.

The Step 7 baseline-retirement lifecycle (SKILL.md:124-132, Loop T7) closes a rot loop nearly every process ignores — intentionally-red characterization tests polluting the next session's preflight — with a carve-out from hard rule 1 that is narrowly scoped (INTENDED-only, post-verdict, same citation, own commit) and defended against abuse in the failure-modes list (SKILL.md:147).

The UNVERIFIED-never-blank discipline is applied consistently across surfaces: env-parity rows ('a blank cell reads as checked-and-clean', SKILL.md:114), missing headless browser (Loop T5 prerequisite), reduced mode (Loop T6), and the capability-detection table (host-adapters.md:20) — honest uncertainty reporting is the phase's genuine differentiator for the non-expert audience.

The asymmetric security cap with articulated reasoning ('A leaked key is not recoverable by trying again tomorrow, so this is the one place the suite refuses to make the trade', loops.md:81) is the right exception to the otherwise-bounded loop design.

The narrow suite-diff exclusion for INTENDED-red baseline tests (SKILL.md:70) anticipates a subtle false-regression interaction between the baseline mechanism and preflight diffing, and bounds the exclusion explicitly so it cannot widen into a loophole.
grokbit-test.summary: grokbit-test's core design is genuinely strong — baseline-before-change characterization, structural verification/repair separation, the UNVERIFIED-never-blank honesty contract, and the Step 7 retirement lifecycle are things most real teams lack. The failures concentrate at the seams: the UNKNOWN classification the skill actively promotes has no consumer at the verdict and its promised hand-back path does not exist (BLOCKER); failing done-criteria force neither a verdict nor an intake; Loop T4's repair, acknowledgment, and rescan machinery points at mechanisms that are never defined; and repeated verify passes have no artifact-versioning model, so hand-back cycles overwrite their own evidence. Two operational-safety slips undercut the phase's own safety posture: the prescribed kubectl invocation prints Secret values, and 'start the real production command' carries no isolation or teardown guidance. For the declared vibe-coder audience, the biggest fit problems are an undefined standalone entry (no path when plan artifacts don't exist) and zero proportionality — the full expensive-tier battery runs identically for a one-line change, which is the strongest incentive to skip the safety net entirely.

findings.title: Loop D1 is a deadlock on the primary audience's machine: it can neither pass nor safely run, and the two texts defining its exit contradict each other
findings.detail: loops.md defines D1's formal exit as 'zero BLOCKER findings' (L30) but then states 'A cap-3 pass counts only if commands were actually executed. Listing them three times and calling it verification is not this loop' (L49-51), and host-adapters.md states flatly that without a disposable container 'Loop D1 cannot exit clean' (L20). Cap behavior is 'block. Do not emit the document' (loops.md L32). Six of twelve seeded types carry commands_run (readme, contributing, runbook, user-guide, test-plan, api-reference). The declared audience is a vibe coder clicking a button in VS Code on their own laptop — no container, no CI. Strict reading: every command-bearing doc (i.e., the skill's own stated most-common request, the README) hits cap 3 and is permanently blocked. Loose reading: an agent exits on the formal 'zero BLOCKER' criterion with all-PENDING results and ships a doc whose 'single highest-value check' (SKILL.md L99) never ran. The only third option the text offers is passing --i-understand-this-runs-shell, which roles.md itself declares unsafe ('never treat a --execute run outside a disposable environment as safe just because the flag exists', L82). No safe degradation path (e.g., 'ship with commands visibly marked UNVERIFIED') is defined anywhere; SKILL.md L99 explicitly forbids the ship-with-warning path. A fix must pick one: define a container-provisioning step, or define an honest degraded emission mode, and make loops.md's Exit line and prose agree.
findings.evidence: A cap-3 pass counts only if commands were actually executed. ... Cap behavior: block. Do not emit the document. / host-adapters.md L20: Commands stay listed, not run, and Loop D1 cannot exit clean

findings.title: Regenerating a previously-emitted doc silently destroys the user's hand edits — the frontmatter-presence rule contradicts 'treat their edit as authoritative'
findings.detail: registry.md § Living documents: 'If the output path already carries this skill's own grokbit_type frontmatter, it was written by this skill before and is safe to regenerate in place' (L87). The diff-and-confirm protection applies only to files with NO frontmatter. But host-adapters.md L95-97 tells the extension to 'Let the user edit any emitted document ... treat their edit as authoritative, the same rule the rest of this suite applies to every artifact.' A user edit does not remove the grokbit_type frontmatter, and authored_sections tracks only Step-3 gap answers, not post-emit manual edits — so nothing distinguishes a pristine emitted doc from a hand-tuned one. The destroy path is fully wired: emit README → user tunes it → source drifts → check_drift.py's own report says 'Regenerate with grokbit-document' (print_report, L305) → regeneration overwrites in place with no diff, no confirmation. This is the one place in the skill that can destroy user work, and it is reached by following the skill's own advice. Fix: record a content hash at emit time (in the manifest the skill already promises but never writes — see separate finding) and route any hash mismatch through the same diff-and-confirm path as a human-authored file.
findings.evidence: If the output path already carries this skill's own `grokbit_type` frontmatter, it was written by this skill before and is safe to regenerate in place.

findings.title: The process requires executing destructive documented commands — a runbook's rollback and migration commands — and CI auto-detection waives the safety acknowledgment exactly where deploy secrets live
findings.detail: types/runbook.md requires verify: [commands_run, ...] (L33) and its body mandates real rollback commands from plan tasks (L40: 'Every rollback command comes from a plan task's rollback field'). Loop D1 requires those commands 'actually executed' to pass (loops.md L49). So verifying a runbook means running rollback/migration commands against whatever environment is present. verify_doc.py's looks_containerized() (L118-121) treats any of CI/CONTAINER/REMOTE_CONTAINERS/CODESPACES env vars as license to --execute with no acknowledgment flag — but a CI runner is disposable only in filesystem terms; it typically holds deploy tokens, DB credentials, and network reach, so 'rollback the migration' can hit a real database. The one guard, the <!-- doc-verify:skip --> fence directive, is opt-in per fence and is mentioned only in verify_doc.py's docstring (L26-28); neither SKILL.md, loops.md, roles.md, nor types/runbook.md instructs the Technical Writer to mark destructive commands — and marking them all would in turn re-trigger the D1 deadlock (commands never 'actually executed'). A world-class process would classify commands (read-only probe vs mutating vs long-running) before execution and require skip-marking of mutating commands as a lint, not an optional courtesy.
findings.evidence: verify: [commands_run, paths_resolve] ... 'Every rollback command comes from a plan task's `rollback` field' — combined with verify_doc.py L121: return any(os.environ.get(v) for v in ("CI", "CONTAINER", ...))

findings.title: emit_at phase hooks and the extension's Documentation picker/coverage preview are fictional — nothing in the suite or the shipped extension implements either
findings.detail: registry.md defines emit_at: 'plan-approval', 'implement-handoff', 'test-verdict' (L58), and adr.md (L44 'Emit at plan approval, while the reasoning is fresh') and changelog.md (L43 'Emit at implement handoff. Written three weeks later this becomes archaeology') stake their whole value on those hooks. Grep of grokbit-plan, grokbit-implement, grokbit-test, and grokbit-explore finds zero references to grokbit-document, emit_at, or any of the three hook names — no phase ever fires them, so every 'derived' type is in practice on-request archaeology, the exact failure its own body text warns about. Likewise SKILL.md's 'Extension (primary)' entry point (L14: invokes with {type_id, slug, target_path} from a Documentation icon) and registry.md's Extension contract (L89-98: enumerate types, compute coverage badges, invoke) describe UI the shipped extension does not have — per the project's own map, the capability surface renders only five workflow tiles that seed the composer with slash text; there is no picker, no coverage computation, no typed invocation. That matters beyond staleness: SKILL.md L79 calls the coverage preview 'the honest replacement for the conversational necessity gate that the click removed' — the safety story for one-click generation rests on a preview that never happens. Either wire the hooks/picker or rewrite these files to describe the natural-language path as primary.
findings.evidence: **`emit_at`** wires the type to a phase boundary. `plan-approval`, `implement-handoff`, `test-verdict`, or `on-request`. — no other skill in resources/skills/ mentions grokbit-document or any of these hook names (verified by grep)

findings.title: Provenance is undefined for uncommitted sources, and the suite's own happy path produces docs that fail its own CI gate forever
findings.detail: provenance.md L20 defines derived_from as '<path>@<commit> — the commit the content was read at.' Nothing anywhere defines what the Documentation Engineer records when the source is untracked or modified in the working tree — which is the NORMAL state of .grokbit/plans/** at document time: the suite never commits automatically (host repo convention), documents are emitted immediately after implement/test, and this very repo's git status shows its plan directories as untracked ('?? .grokbit/plans/...'). The two possible behaviors are both defective: (a) record no/any sha → check_drift.py reports 'untracked' or 'unknown-commit', and FAIL_STATUSES (L71) plus '--ci exits 1 when any finding of any status exists' (docstring L37) means CI is permanently red for a correctly-generated doc; (b) record HEAD's sha while reading dirty content → git diff recorded..HEAD compares committed states only, so genuine drift between the read content and the committed content is invisible — the provenance lies. roles.md's Documentation Engineer ('capture both the content and the source commit', L37) gives no instruction for either case. A world-class pipeline defines this: e.g., record @worktree with a content hash, or block emission until sources are committed.
findings.evidence: `derived_from` is `<path>@<commit>` — the commit the content was read at, not the commit the doc was written at. — vs check_drift.py L71: FAIL_STATUSES = {"drifted", "deleted", "untracked", "unknown-commit", ...}

findings.title: verify_doc.py grades unresolvable paths MAJOR while loops.md D1 declares them BLOCKER — broken paths ship and D1 exits clean anyway
findings.detail: loops.md D1 body item 2 (L22-23) enumerates BLOCKER defects: 'a command that failed, a path or link that doesn't resolve, a broken anchor, a cited source that doesn't exist, a code sample that doesn't parse.' But check_paths emits Finding("path", "MAJOR", ...) (verify_doc.py L240), and main() computes the failing exit solely from severity == "BLOCKER" (L476, L499). So a doc referencing `src/auth/reset.ts` when the file is actually `src/auth/reset-token.ts` produces a MAJOR, exit code 0, D1's 'zero BLOCKER findings' exit is satisfied on pass one, and the doc ships — directly contradicting the loop's promise that path resolution has 'teeth.' (Aggravating: check_paths only inspects backtick-quoted inline tokens matching a narrow regex, L85, so paths in prose or tables are never checked at all, which loops.md never discloses.) Either promote path findings to BLOCKER or rewrite loops.md's defect list to match the script; today an agent following loops.md and an agent trusting the script's exit code reach opposite verdicts on the same document.
findings.evidence: out.append(Finding("path", "MAJOR", f"path does not resolve: {p}", line)) — vs loops.md L22-23: 'Every `BLOCKER` finding is a defect: a command that failed, a path or link that doesn't resolve...'

findings.title: Six of twelve seeded types fall below the registry's own declared verification floor — the README's provenance is never checked by D1
findings.detail: registry.md L60 declares '[links_follow, citations_valid]' the floor: 'every type derives from *something* and can cite or link something, even a mostly-authored one, so those two checks are the floor.' But an explicit per-type verify list overrides the default, and the seeded types drop below it: readme (L33) and user-guide (L30) omit citations_valid; contributing (L32) and runbook (L33) omit BOTH citations_valid and links_follow; test-plan (L36) and api-reference (L26) omit links_follow. Consequences: the flagship README — the type hard rule 4 ('Every derived document carries provenance') most needs to hold for — can ship with a derived_from citing a nonexistent artifact and D1 never notices (check_drift only helps later, and only for statuses, not at emission); a 2am runbook ships with broken markdown links unchecked, for the one reader least able to route around them. Either the floor is real (make verify additive above it) or it is not (delete the claim); as written the registry's data contradicts the registry's prose.
findings.evidence: verify: [commands_run, paths_resolve] — vs registry.md L60: 'those two checks are the floor' ([links_follow, citations_valid])

findings.title: Loop D2 has contradictory instructions for the no-isolation host and an unactionable definition of 'attempt the task' — its exit can be satisfied vacuously
findings.detail: host-adapters.md L15 says on hosts without isolated subagents to 'Run roles sequentially; write-then-re-read between roles' including for D2, while roles.md L86 orders the opposite: 'If you have context from any of those, you cannot perform this check and should say so rather than performing it badly.' An agent on a single-context host cannot obey both; and if it obeys roles.md, loops.md defines no outcome for a D2 that never ran — 'Exit: zero BLOCKER findings' (L78) is trivially true of an unperformed check, so the skill's second-highest-value gate silently becomes a no-op with no Known-gaps note (cap behavior only covers surviving findings, not an unrun test). Separately, the isolated reviewer gets 'only the document and a clean environment' (SKILL.md L105) and must 'attempt the task the document describes' — but a README/user-guide task requires the repo, the app, and the network, none of which the reviewer has, so the 'attempt' is necessarily a mental walkthrough while the spec's language ('attempts', 'clean environment') claims execution. Define: (a) the precedence between the two instructions, (b) an explicit D2-SKIPPED outcome that itself forces a visible note in the emitted doc, (c) what the reviewer actually does (structured walkthrough audit), so the check's evidence class is honest.
findings.evidence: Run roles sequentially; write-then-re-read between roles. Loop D2 (the fresh-reader test) needs this the most — vs roles.md L86: 'If you have context from any of those, you cannot perform this check and should say so rather than performing it badly.'

findings.title: authored_sections' promised differential drift treatment is unimplemented — the exact 'advertised but silently absent' defect class the registry boasts of having eliminated
findings.detail: provenance.md L22-23: 'Drift detection must treat these differently: they cannot be regenerated, so a changed source means *review this*, not *rerun the generator*.' roles.md's Documentation Engineer repeats it (L43-44: 'drift detection has to treat them differently'). check_drift.py never reads authored_sections — the string does not appear in the script; findings carry no authored/derived distinction, and print_report's uniform closing advice is 'Regenerate with grokbit-document, or re-verify and bump the commit' (L305) — i.e., precisely the 'rerun the generator' instruction the design document forbids for authored content, which feeds the regeneration-clobbers-edits BLOCKER above. registry.md L60 explicitly celebrates removing signatures_match rather than leaving a check 'advertised and silently skipped'; this is the same defect left in place. Fix is small: parse authored_sections in check_drift.py, tag findings whose sections intersect it, and split the advice line.
findings.evidence: print("Regenerate with grokbit-document, or re-verify and bump the commit.") — while provenance.md L22 requires 'a changed source means *review this*, not *rerun the generator*' for authored sections; 'authored_sections' appears nowhere in check_drift.py

findings.title: The drift hook's hardcoded path and the 'Single-source install' section describe an install mechanism the product deleted — the hook is silently dead on the shipped install
findings.detail: hooks/doc-drift.json's command runs '.grokbit/skills/grokbit-document/scripts/check_drift.py' (L37), and host-adapters.md § Single-source install (L103-114) documents an install.sh that symlinks .grokbit/skills into .claude/skills and .grok/skills. The shipped product does neither: the extension's provisionSkillSuite copies resources/skills into ~/.grok/skills and ~/.claude/skills (home tier), and install.sh was deliberately deleted in favor of copy-provisioning (per the project map: 'Copy, not symlink, and the deleted install.sh is why'). So a user who follows doc-drift.json's own copy-in instructions on the actual default install gets a command that references a nonexistent script — and the trailing '; true' plus 'never fails loudly' design (comment L27-28) guarantees the failure is invisible forever: the advisory drift check, a headline feature of the Staleness section, silently never runs. The comment's 'Adjust if you installed this skill somewhere else' (L23) inverts reality — the documented canonical location is the one that doesn't exist. Update the default path to the provisioned home-tier location and delete or rewrite the Single-source install section.
findings.evidence: "command": "PY=$(command -v python3 || ...); [ -n \"$PY\" ] && \"$PY\" .grokbit/skills/grokbit-document/scripts/check_drift.py --hook; true" — a path only the deleted install.sh layout (host-adapters.md L103-114) ever created

findings.title: verify_doc.py executes bash/zsh blocks with the platform default shell and a flat 120s timeout — correct quickstarts fail as BLOCKERs and block emission
findings.detail: run() gives powershell/cmd explicit interpreters but for every SCRIPT_LANGS block falls through to 'argv, shell = script, True' (L379-380): on Linux CI — the environment the skill steers execution toward — shell=True is /bin/sh, which on Ubuntu is dash, so a valid ```bash block using [[ ]], arrays, or process substitution exits non-zero; on Windows it is cmd.exe, where a multi-line POSIX script is garbage. Each false failure is a BLOCKER (L417), and D1's cap behavior is 'do not emit' — so a document whose commands genuinely work when a human runs them is permanently blocked by interpreter mismatch, the inverse of the defect the check exists to catch. Separately, the default 120s timeout (L437) makes any long-running quickstart command — 'npm run dev', 'docker compose up', every serve/watch command, i.e. the archetypal first command of a README — time out into a BLOCKER; the only escape is doc-verify:skip, which un-verifies the doc's single most important command with no middle ground (start, probe, kill). Fix: dispatch bash/zsh blocks to the declared interpreter when present (bash -c / zsh -c), and add a directive or heuristic for long-running commands (e.g. doc-verify:background with a liveness probe).
findings.evidence:
else:
        argv, shell = script, True — sh/bash/shell/zsh blocks all run under /bin/sh (dash on Ubuntu CI) or cmd.exe on Windows, never the declared interpreter

findings.title: The output contract promises .grokbit/docs-manifest.json that no step, role, or script ever writes — and the registry schema carries a coverage_source field defined nowhere and read by nothing
findings.detail: SKILL.md's Output contract (L137) lists '.grokbit/docs-manifest.json  type → path → provenance → last verified', and provenance.md § Manifest (L54-56) instructs the extension to render the doc set from it and CI to 'check completeness against the registry.' But Step 7 — the emission step — writes only the document and the .grokbit/context digest (L111-124); no role in roles.md owns the manifest, and neither script reads or writes it (check_drift discovers docs by walking DEFAULT_SCAN_PATHS, verify_doc takes explicit paths). Consumers are pointed at a file that never exists. In the same class: every type's frontmatter carries coverage_source (e.g. registry.md schema L18, readme.md L9), but the registry's field notes define every other field and never this one, and nothing in SKILL.md, roles.md, or the scripts consumes it — Step 2's coverage is computed from per-section derive_from, making coverage_source dead, undefined data in all twelve types. Both violate the registry's own stated discipline (L60: nothing advertised is 'left advertised and silently skipped'). Either add manifest emission to Step 7 (it is also the natural home for the content hash the regeneration BLOCKER needs) and define coverage_source, or delete both.

strengths: The no-sandbox honesty around command execution is genuinely rare and correct: verify_doc.py's SAFETY docstring (scripts/verify_doc.py L16-28) states plainly that --execute 'runs shell commands extracted from a text file, with the full inherited environment and network — there is no sandbox, and this script does not build one', and gates it behind container detection or an explicit scary flag rather than pretending safety.

'Listed is not verified' is enforced mechanically, not rhetorically: unexecuted commands are a distinct PENDING severity, a distinct exit code 3, and a printed warning ('Commands were listed, not run — this is NOT the same as verified', scripts/verify_doc.py L492-497, L499-502) — most doc tooling silently conflates the two.

Differentiated cap behavior with stated reasoning (references/loops.md L3-7, L87-91): D1 (machine-checkable) blocks at cap, D2 (judgment) ships with a visible dated 'Known gaps' note — matching enforcement strength to evidence class instead of applying one cap policy everywhere.

Every seeded type's derive_from anchor actually resolves against the sibling skills' templates (verified: intent/survey/design/plan/review templates in grokbit-plan/assets, preflight/handoff/progress in grokbit-implement/assets, baseline/results/security/release-readiness in grokbit-test/assets) — the cross-skill data contract is real, not aspirational, and registry.md L108 even warns custom-type authors to check it.

Per-type writing guidance is unusually good craft: runbook's 'organise by symptom, not by component' (types/runbook.md L38), changelog's reader-side framing (types/changelog.md L37), the ADR numbered-file collision rule with never-overwrite (references/registry.md L43), and security-posture's 'never restate a secret, even redacted, even rotated' (types/security-posture.md L42).

No handling of long-running or interactive commands: the only options are execute-until-120s-timeout (false BLOCKER) or doc-verify:skip (unverified). A real doc-testing harness has a start/probe/kill pattern for servers and a way to feed canned stdin — quickstarts are dominated by exactly these commands.

No suite-level consistency pass: each document is verified in isolation, but nothing ever checks that README, user-guide, api-reference, and contributing agree with each other on terminology, versions, or duplicated quickstart steps — cross-doc contradiction is a staleness mode drift detection structurally cannot see (both docs cite unchanged sources yet disagree).

Drift is measured only against HEAD (git diff recorded..HEAD): there is no released-version semantics, so a doc that is correct for the shipped tag reads 'drifted' the moment main moves, and a doc regenerated from main is wrong for every user on the release — no versioned-docs story at all.

No screenshot/image lifecycle: user guides are the type most dependent on UI captures, KNOWN_EXTS even recognizes png/jpg for path resolution, yet nothing captures, verifies, or staleness-tracks images — the fastest-rotting artifact in end-user documentation.

No partial-regeneration/merge strategy: regeneration is all-or-nothing over the whole file, with no 'regenerate only the sections whose sources drifted, preserve the rest' path — which is both what makes in-place regeneration dangerous (finding 2) and what claim-level drift detection naturally sets up but never cashes in.

No deterministic prose gate: the suite prizes 'a script, not model work' for checkable facts, yet ships no style/reading-level/terminology lint (vale-class) even though 02-survey conventions give it a ready terminology source — and security-posture's 'never restate a secret' rule is prompt-only, with no secret-pattern scan over emitted docs at D1 time.
grokbit-document.summary: grokbit-document's design instincts are well above typical LLM-workflow boilerplate: it correctly identifies verification and provenance as the actual product, is unusually honest about its own tooling limits (no sandbox, listed-is-not-verified, under-reporting section attribution), and its cross-skill derive_from data contract genuinely resolves against the sibling templates. But its enforcement layer contradicts itself exactly where everything hinges: Loop D1 is a deadlock-or-unsafe-flag dilemma on the primary audience's machine (no container means it can never validly pass, and cap behavior is 'never emit'), the regenerate-in-place rule silently destroys user hand-edits while check_drift's own output tells users to trigger it, and D1's mandatory execution of runbook rollback/migration commands — with CI env vars waiving the safety acknowledgment — is a destroy-user-data path dressed as verification. A second tier of defects is 'advertised but unimplemented' wiring: emit_at phase hooks and the extension picker/coverage preview exist in no other skill or shipped surface, authored_sections' promised drift treatment is absent from check_drift.py, the docs-manifest is promised and never written, the drift hook's default path points at a deleted install layout, and six of twelve seeded types fall below the registry's own declared verification floor. The scripts themselves are the strongest artifacts in the skill but diverge from what loops.md claims they enforce (path findings graded MAJOR not BLOCKER; bash blocks run under /bin/sh or cmd.exe). Net: a thoughtfully argued process whose written guarantees a careful reader cannot currently trust end-to-end — closer to world-class in philosophy than in enforcement.

gaps.gap: No use of the suite's own memory as an orientation source: grokbit-plan Step 0 reads .grokbit/handoff.md because "a previous session may already have answered half of what you are about to ask" (plan SKILL.md:34), and .grokbit/plans/** holds prior cited surveys/designs — the highest-value orientation material in a repo the suite has touched — yet Explore never mentions reading either. The orientation phase runs blind to the suite's own prior orientation.

No cross-session durability, in a host whose UX makes new sessions the norm: the map is chat-only and the Grokbit extension opens one session per tab, so an Explore map is unrecoverable the moment the user opens a fresh tab to plan. The skill forbids REQUIRING durable digests (correct) but never even offers an optional one-paragraph handoff note (e.g. appending to .grokbit/handoff.md, which Plan already reads), so the phase's entire output evaporates at the suite's most common session boundary.

No secrets hygiene: exploration naturally opens .env files, credential configs, and CI secrets, and nothing forbids quoting their values (or even flagging their paths) into the chat map — which persists in on-disk session history (chat_history.jsonl / Claude .jsonl). A world-class read-only phase has an explicit redaction rule: cite the path, never the content, of anything credential-shaped.

No use of version-control history as an orientation instrument: git log/blame for churn hot-spots, recent authorship, and commit messages around the charter area is standard world-class orientation practice (often faster and more reliable than reading cold source), is read-only by nature, and is never mentioned.

No guidance for degenerate repos: an empty/greenfield repo, a repo with no README/docs, or a non-code question ("what does this product do?") — the Cartographer's entry-point heuristic (README, module map, main packages) assumes a mature codebase and the skill defines no honest behavior when those don't exist.

No output-size bound or summary-first structure for the chat map: every loop is capped but the deliverable itself is not — nothing stops a 200-bullet 'Relevant areas' wall, which for a vibe-coder audience defeats the orientation purpose as surely as an uncited map. World-class practice: a hard bullet budget or a two-tier map (five-line summary, details below).

No security or privacy thinking at design time: the design template's risk surface is the unhappy-path table (network failure, empty state, concurrent edit, permission denied) and a migration section — no threat consideration, authZ-change review, secrets handling, or input-validation requirement. The suite defers all security to grokbit-test's post-implementation pass, which is exactly when design-level security flaws are most expensive to fix. A world-class team does security review at the design gate.

No repo-state anchoring or staleness contract: 02-survey.md citations are not pinned to a git SHA and nothing detects the repository changing between survey, approval, and implement start. A plan approved Friday against Monday's very different tree presents the same confident citations. World-class: record HEAD at survey time and have implement's preflight diff against it.

No plan-time smoke-check that the verify harness itself exists: Loop 4 validates verify: commands purely by inspection against the survey's conventions section. No quality bar on rollbacks for stateful changes: the checklist requires only 'Has a rollback', and the template's example is 'git revert <commit>' — which does not un-apply a database migration, un-send an email, or un-publish a package. The design template asks 'Reversible:' for migrations but nothing forces the corresponding task's rollback: field to be a real down-migration. A world-class plan distinguishes code rollback from state rollback per task.

No non-functional requirements capture: the intent template's done-criteria are purely functional/observable; there is no prompt for performance budgets, accessibility, i18n, or observability (logging/metrics for the new code path), so the Reviewer has no basis to flag their absence and the plan cannot fail for lacking them.

No rollout/exposure planning for risky changes: no concept of feature flags, staged enablement, or kill switches even when the design's own migration section admits a mixed-version window — the plan goes from approval to full deployment of behavior with no intermediate exposure state.

No post-approval integrity protection on plan.md: the human's approval checkbox (plan.template.md:85) is a mutable markdown line with no snapshot or hash of what was approved; nothing distinguishes the approved text from later agent edits, so 'the human approved this plan' is unverifiable after the fact.

No estimation or risk-ranking of tasks: blast radius is a single header line (N files, N deps, schema y/n); individual tasks carry no risk or size signal beyond the ~200-line guide, so the human at the gate cannot see which of twelve tasks is the dangerous one — a world-class gate presentation leads with it.

No code-quality review exists anywhere in the phase: the Code Reviewer is explicitly scope-only ('You are not reviewing code quality in general', roles.md:78), so logic errors, missing edge cases, and poor error handling that happen to pass the single verify command ship unreviewed — a world-class team reviews the change itself, not just its boundary.

No branch isolation or whole-plan abandonment procedure: every task commits directly to the user's current branch, so a DO NOT SHIP verdict or an abandoned session leaves N unshippable commits on (typically) main with no defined unwind beyond per-task `git revert` — a world-class team implements on a branch where abandonment is deleting it.

No safety screening of plan-authored verify commands before execution: Implement runs `verify:` verbatim up to three times; a destructive command (rm -rf, git clean, db reset) that survived plan approval by a non-expert executes unchecked — a world-class process lints or sandboxes commands it did not write.

Dependency-gate trigger coverage is a hardcoded three-command list ('Any npm install, pip install, cargo add', SKILL.md:75): yarn/pnpm/bun/poetry/uv/go get are ungated, and editing package.json directly followed by a bare `npm install` bypasses the gate entirely; the gate also never mandates --ignore-scripts or post-install lockfile pinning, so an approved package's install scripts still run arbitrary code.

No flaky-test or quarantine policy anywhere: nothing distinguishes 'red because broken' from 'red because flaky' — no rerun rule, no stability check at baseline commit time, no quarantine list carried between sessions.

No test-adequacy measure for NEW code: the phase checks stated done-criteria and old behavior (baseline replay), but new logic paths that have neither a criterion nor a pre-existing behavior are never required to be exercised — no changed-line coverage, branch coverage, or mutation check on the diff.
